title: Reading music versus playing by ear
summary: Raymond Burke, Harry Shields and George Lewis did not read; the cradle of jazz was not apparent to Sid.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I thought there was as much of that type music or that style of music played everywhere else. And it wasn't some time later that we found out that this was where the thing started from and what do we call it, the cradle of jazz. And most styles, and this style evolved from New Orleans and was carried up north by some musicians, you know. But no, I wasn't conscious of that. I just thought everybody should do it that way and everybody did it that way. You'd see a guy, and what it raised me when I first began to play music, I'd speak with some musicians somewhere, find out that they couldn't read music. And how do you play so well? How do you do it, you see? I guess I don't have the greatest ear in the world because, or else I started on the wrong hand. These guys, a lot of these guys started reading music, such as myself. Some guys just picked up the horn and started playing it, you know. Now Raymond Burke would give me an argument every time, you know. Raymond, I said, well, you don't read music at all? And he said, no. And I'd say, well, it would kind of open, I think they would kind of broaden your feeling and broaden your horizon a little bit if you could read, even sparingly, even hulkily. He said, that would interfere with my improvisation. He said, I refuse to learn how to read music. And Harry Shields was of that, too. Harry Shields would do that all the time. You see, we had Sharky in here. Sharky worked for us a while with Harry Shields, George Brunis, and Jake Martin. And Harry would give you that argument. He thought that if he learned to read any music, it would be more of a hindrance and it would be a help. And perhaps so, because, but perhaps not. Perhaps not. Mike broadened his understanding of harmony. Yeah. Broadened his scope of harmony.

Very difficult to say, some of those guys who were, or like Bunk Johnson, for instance, was a trumpet player. He could read music. He was a good reader. And others, you see, like George Lewis could never read music.
No, he'd never, he'd never learned to read music at all. He didn't seem to make too much difference. So I guess there's no real rules about it.

I don't think so, no. I like to believe that it would broaden, if you broaden your knowledge about what you're doing in some sense, that the feel might become larger and you could feel more free to move around harmonically, you know. But then again, too, if you start thinking about what you're doing, sometimes you don't do it as well, you know.
I think it's a good thing, particularly a thing that you should do naturally, and essentially just playing music, I guess. You either got a feel for it or you don't have.
